Stated Claim / Post Context:
Our Republican Legacy (ORL) Policy Statement in Support of Ukraine Against Russian Aggression

ORL strongly supports Ukraine against Russia’s illegal war. We oppose the Administration’s unwillingness to support Ukraine’s ability to negotiate from a position of military and economic strength against Russia and the administration’s refusal to include Ukraine in the talks regarding Ukraine’s own fate.

Actual Article Body:
Home

About Us

ORL Team

The Latest

Policy Statements

More

The issue. The Trump Administration has reversed U.S. policy on Ukraine in the face of Russia’s illegal invasion and ongoing aggression. Despite his campaign promise to end the war in Ukraine on his first day in office, President Trump has failed to stop the killing of this horrific conflict.

The Trump Administration continues to exhibit bias for Russia and against Ukraine. It has halted and denied Ukraine military and economic aid, and temporarily halted sharing vital intelligence information critical for Ukraine’s defense.  It votes with Russia and North Korea against Ukraine in the United Nations. These actions favor Russia the aggressor not Ukraine the victim.

When conducting peace negotiations with Russia, the Administration failed to include Ukraine or its European allies.  Russia continues its morbid tradition of violating treaties, agreements, and even cease-fires without consequences, as notably demonstrated on Easter Sunday and the end of Passover.

The U.S. negotiations so far are unproductive and one-sided in favor of Russia. Russia has no incentives to pursue peace or retreat from its current positions in Ukraine, as long as the Trump Administration assumes a position of weakness not strength.  By its actions and inaction, the Trump Administration has failed to protect our national interests in Europe.

ORL policy position. ORL strongly supports Ukraine against Russia’s illegal war. We oppose the Administration’s unwillingness to support Ukraine’s ability to negotiate from a position of military and economic strength against Russia and the administration’s refusal to include Ukraine in the talks regarding Ukraine’s own fate. We support both the United States and Ukraine negotiating from a position of combined strength, not mutual weakness.

ORL believes that strong U.S. military and economic support for Ukraine is in the national economic and security interests of the United States, Ukraine, and all of Europe. For Ukraine, U.S. support will put it in a better negotiating position for any future peace negotiations while also helping it to defend itself during Russia’s escalating aggression.

For the United States, Ukraine is also at the forefront of defending all of Europe from further Russian aggression that would trigger U.S. military intervention pursuant to our NATO Article 5 obligations. The United States also benefits economically from our investment in Ukraine since the vast majority of U.S. military defense spending to help Ukraine stays in the United States and spurs America’s economic growth.

We also support Ukraine joining the European Union and eventually NATO as the ultimate guarantee of its future security.  We agree with the President that European nations should increase their financial and material support for Ukraine, as they directly benefit from Ukraine’s defense of its territorial integrity.

Action required. ORL calls on the Trump Administration and Congress to reaffirm and support U.S. investment in Ukraine’s military and economic security.  Any peace negotiations must include Ukraine and must be from a position of Ukraine’s demonstrable strength.  Specifically, ORL supports:

U.S. military and economic support to help Ukraine defend its sovereignty and citizens against Russian aggression.

Our NATO allies in the common opposition to Russian aggression in Europe, with the commitment that they help defend Ukraine through increased investment and equitable burden sharing.

A just and enduring Ukrainian-Russian peace settlement that guarantees Ukraine’s future sovereignty, territory, democracy, and security without fear of future Russian aggression or intimidation.

The immediate return by Russia of all abducted Ukrainian children before any U.S. sanctions are relaxed or removed.

Taking immediate steps to impose the overwhelming cost of Russia’s aggression on Russia through the transfer of its sovereign assets to Ukraine.

Ensuring Ukraine’s future economic and military security, including its membership in the European Union and eventually in NATO.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
7 Washingtonians share their views on Trump's immigration policy

The Trump administration's immigration crackdown continues to divide Americans, and polls show declining support for the president’s mass deportation campaign. Members of KUOW's Community Voices Network weigh in on Trump's immigration policy.

Actual Article Body:
The Trump administration's immigration crackdown continues to divide Americans, and polls show declining support for the president’s mass deportation campaign.

A recent poll by Fox News found President Donald Trump’s approval rating on immigration now stands at 43%, down five percentage points from last summer. A majority of respondents said immigration enforcement has gone too far.

A September poll by Politico found mass deportations are causing wider divisions within Trump’s base.

Washington state saw a surge of ICE activity this summer, according to KUOW’s recent analysis of ICE datasets obtained by the Deportation Data Project. According to the data, the majority of arrests were of people who had no criminal record.

Seven Washington residents shared their thoughts about the current immigration crackdown. Their participation is part of KUOW’s Community Voices Network, a project that asks a diverse group of community members to weigh in on the big issues of the day.

Read more about why we are investing in this kind of reporting and how we are recruiting people for the project here.

Mark Ibay, 25, Parkland, WA

“I’ve had relatives who were pulled over; they were questioned for hours on end.”

Mark Ibay is a clerk at Western State Hospital. He immigrated from the Philippines to the U.S. in 2019 and became a naturalized citizen in 2025. Even with that status, Ibay says he can’t help but worry.

“I carry my passport card with me wherever I go,” Ibay said. “The current enforcement is really scary.”

He said he understands these efforts are targeted at people with criminal records or those who are here unlawfully, according to the Trump administration. But he said the way it’s carried out seems harsh.

Ibay said the administration’s approach and the way Immigration and Customs Enforcement is carrying out detentions and deportations is having a negative impact on immigrant communities.

“There are a lot of innocent souls out there who also get caught in the crossfire,” he said.

Politically, Ibay considers himself “neutral,” adding that he prefers candidates who will actually do the work and follow up on their plans. He said he’s still trying to learn about his new home and its systems.

“We’re here to build community,” Ibay said. “Because you’ve given us the opportunity, we want to give it back.”

Diana McAllister, 75, Arlington, WA

“It’s one of the things I voted for, was get tough, take a stand, and make it happen.”

Diana McAllister supports the Trump Administration’s deportation efforts — it’s the policy she voted for.

“If they’re not citizens, they don’t have rights in this country. They’ve not paid their dues,” McAllister said. “If they come into this country illegally, they need to go home.”

McAllister is founder of the Family Academy, which educates parents on how to homeschool their children. She said she was once a card-carrying Democrat. Her mother was active in the party; dinner at the family table often included party stalwarts like Warren Magnuson, Scoop Jackson, and Mike Lowry.

Now she describes herself as ultra-conservative. McAllister’s views changed when she had children and decided to homeschool them.

“My ideas, my values changed from ultra-liberal, ‘We need to take care of everybody and give stuff away,’ to ‘No, I want to take care of my own,’” she said.

McAllister understands there are industries that rely on immigrants for labor. At one time she tried to help a local business with visa applications for its workers. She found the process burdensome, but she still believes employers need to make the effort to hire people legally.

“If you’re coming to work and you’re a farmer and you need workers, and these guys are willing to do the job, then do it,” McAllister said. “Register them so they have a background of having been productive and appropriate. Help them in that way.”

Gabriel Dias, 24, Renton, WA

“We’re seeing families torn apart.”

When Gabriel Dias is not working with special needs students as a paraeducator, they monitor ICE enforcement activities as part of a citizens’ rapid-response team.

“We show up to make sure the process is legal and that no one’s rights are being violated,” Dias said.

Dias is a trans woman. They started getting involved in local groups monitoring ICE when they lived in Florida in 2021 to begin transitioning. It was a rough place to be trans or to be an organizer, they said. The following year, Dias moved to Washington state.

“This is a place that I could be myself and continue to help people who need help,” they said. “It wasn’t safe to help people in Florida and I am [able to safely help people] now.”

In an ideal world, Dias said the U.S. would have an immigration system with a legal pathway to citizenship that’s easier for people who are not criminals. For example, the system should have more immigration judges.

Dias said the recent ICE enforcements have been alarming. They noted that the arrests were originally focused on people with criminal records, but now the goal has shifted to include those without criminal records.

“We’re seeing families torn apart,” Dias said. “At what point is it just, ‘We don’t want immigrants anymore.’”

Frank Schin, 82, Vashon Island, WA

“It has gone vastly overboard and vastly wrong.”

Frank Schin considers himself a social conservative, but also as someone who helps those who can’t make it on their own. He voted for Donald Trump once, in 2016.

Schin said for decades, the government has allowed people to cross the borders illegally by looking the other way. He said it’s a good idea to correct that.

“If they have the name of an individual that is here in the country illegally, (and) they are wanted for a serious crime — those people should be arrested and they should be sent back to their country,” Schin said.

But he doesn’t approve of the way the administration is handling the issue and the people it has hired to be enforcers.

“I think the people working on that job have to be screened more carefully,” Schin said. “They can’t find people and so they were taking anybody and they weren’t checking the credentials of some of these people.”

Schin said he’s not against people coming to the country, especially to fill positions in industries that need them, including health care and agriculture.

“We need to get more people in here to help us, but we also need to secure the border,” he said. “So, there’s some tough situations to decide how you do it.”

Cheryl Hanson, 57, Renton, WA

“The old adage of treating people the way you want to be treated is something that has been infused in me as a child and that really influences the way I think about immigration.”

The vast majority of Cheryl Hanson’s career has been recruiting for tech companies and philanthropic organizations. Many of the people she has helped hire were from other countries.

“Even if we did only hire from U.S. universities… we would have to consider students who were from other countries,” Hanson said. “Because so many of our graduate programs in highly specialized areas cannot find enough students that are U.S. citizens to apply for these positions and pay tuition for our universities.”

Hanson said she’s alarmed by how ICE enforcements have been carried out, saying they’re neither humane nor democratic.

“I do understand the need for ensuring that we are not allowing people into the country who are terrorists or murderers,” Hanson said. “The reality is that immigrants comprise a much lower percentage of crimes than the overall population.”

Hanson said her perspective toward immigrants is shaped in part by her family history. Her grandfather was initially denied entry to the United States after fleeing Poland in the 1920s. But he entered anyway. Hanson believes that had he gone back, he would’ve perished in the Holocaust.

“I wouldn’t exist if he hadn’t been allowed into the U.S,” Hanson said. “I’m eternally grateful that he made it here, eventually became a citizen, and built a family and business and contributed to [the] community.”

Levi Sweeney, 30, Skyway, WA

“I keep saying, immigration is not my number one problem, but I've never met an immigrant I didn't like.”

Levi Sweeney refers to himself as a “dyed-in-the-wool Republican.” He voted for Trump in 2024, although not with much enthusiasm. He calls Trump “the best of a bunch of bad options.”

Sweeney currently works as a janitor in his family’s printing business. He is also a writer and self-publishes his novels.

He said he believes immigration policy under Trump is “going in the right direction, more or less.” He describes the Biden administration immigration policy as “lax.”

He believes “illegal immigrants who are career criminals should absolutely be deported.”

But he is more circumspect about people who are in the country without authorization but who “have a clean record, who are just regular guys and gals, who have held down jobs and contributed to their community.”

“[They] should of course be given leniency,” he said.

But that would mean changing immigration policies to allow for workers to come to the U.S. legally, Sweeney said.

“I would love it if they could live in this country legally, and could easily migrate here without breaking any laws,” he said.

Sweeney doesn’t believe that many people voted for President Trump because he promised to crack down on illegal immigration. He believes most were concerned about bread and butter issues, like the economy, jobs, and housing.

In terms of the people who are being arrested on the streets by ICE, he said it's unfortunate.

“I'd prefer it didn't have to happen at all, to be frank,” he said.

Leona Oliveros, 33, Federal Way, WA

“The movement of people is usually part of a bigger system, bigger injustice that we might not be able to see individually… but it’s there.”

As a history teacher, immigration is top of mind for Leona Oliveros. She teaches at Highline College where about a third of the students enrolled are not U.S.-born citizens.

Oliveros said she makes room for them to talk about their families’ immigration stories to help them see there’s no standard experience.

“Some of my students, there can be tension when talking about immigration, legal versus illegal, like, ‘Why would you do it this way, I had to do it the legal way?’” she said.

That sentiment resonates within her family, according to Oliveros. Like many of her older family members, her parents came to the U.S. from the Philippines by enlisting in the military; it was a pathway to citizenship.

“There’s this assumption that all other undocumented immigration is like jumping the border and the desert and not having the empathy to see that it’s not as simple as that,” she said.

Oliveros sees how current ICE enforcements are affecting students on campus. When word gets out about potential ICE sightings or activities around the area, students don’t come to school or they worry about how to get to work.

“I hate seeing that kind of anxiety among my student body,” Oliveros said. “What’s the American dream if we’re also making it harder to do?”

'They’re all gone!' White House 'bot' supporters AWOL after Russian data center hit

Supporters of the White House barely showed up in replies to its latest post about election fraud, as critics claimed its “bots” vanished after drones hit a Russian data center.“Under President Trump, criminals who disrupt the integrity of America’s elections will be prosecuted to the fullest extent...

Actual Article Body:
Supporters of the White House barely showed up in replies to its latest post about election fraud, as critics claimed its “bots” vanished after drones hit a Russian data center.

“Under President Trump, criminals who disrupt the integrity of America’s elections will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” the White House wrote on X Monday.

The post shared a Justice Department announcement of charges against 16 people accused of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration and related election crimes.

A Raw Story review of the 176 most relevant replies Monday found that 138 opposed or mocked the White House. Only 19 backed it, and 19 more could not be classified.

“So Trump and Elon are going to jail?” one user asked.

“Hey! Where’d all the bots go?!?” another user wrote.

“Are you sad your RUSSIAN bot farms were destroyed?” a third user asked.

“Sixteen down, tens of thousands to go!” wrote one of the few users who backed the White House.

“Holy s— read the comments. The bots are completely gone,” Quadcarl, an X user with nearly 48,000 followers, wrote 22 minutes after the White House posted.

“Lmao usually these posts are filled with bootlicking bots….they’re all gone!” wrote the account Wu Tang is for the Children, which has more than 300,000 followers.

Their posts on X show the claim spread among popular accounts, but the posts are not evidence that it is true.

“Now that Russia data centers are getting pounded by Ukraine, your bots are going away,” another user replied to the White House.

Yandex, a Russian tech company sometimes called “Russia’s Google,” said Sunday that a drone attack completely shut down its data center in the Vladimir region, Reuters reported.

It was the third major Yandex data center knocked out in a few days, after strikes on sites in Sasovo and Kaluga, according to Reuters.

Yandex has blamed Ukraine for the Kaluga attack, but Ukraine has not officially claimed the strikes, The Deep Dive reported.

Automated traffic from Yandex’s network fell to near zero around the start of Oct. 11, according to Cloudflare Radar data cited by The Deep Dive. At one point that day, requests stood at 0.3% of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2% at the same hour a week earlier.

The Deep Dive writer JP Alegre cautioned that knocking out so much of Yandex’s infrastructure would likely cut automated requests even if no influence operation ran there.

“The chart can’t separate fewer bots from fewer working servers,” Alegre wrote.

“If they have the name of an individual that is here in the country illegally, (and) they are wanted for a serious crime — those people should be arrested and they should be sent back to their country,” Schin said.

But he doesn’t approve of the way the administration is handling the issue and the people it has hired to be enforcers.

“I think the people working on that job have to be screened more carefully,” Schin said. “They can’t find people and so they were taking anybody and they weren’t checking the credentials of some of these people.”

Schin said he’s not against people coming to the country, especially to fill positions in industries that need them, including health care and agriculture.

“We need to get more people in here to help us, but we also need to secure the border,” he said. “So, there’s some tough situations to decide how you do it.”

Cheryl Hanson, 57, Renton, WA

“The old adage of treating people the way you want to be treated is something that has been infused in me as a child and that really influences the way I think about immigration.”

The vast majority of Cheryl Hanson’s career has been recruiting for tech companies and philanthropic organizations. Many of the people she has helped hire were from other countries.

“Even if we did only hire from U.S. universities… we would have to consider students who were from other countries,” Hanson said. “Because so many of our graduate programs in highly specialized areas cannot find enough students that are U.S. citizens to apply for these positions and pay tuition for our universities.”

Hanson said she’s alarmed by how ICE enforcements have been carried out, saying they’re neither humane nor democratic.

“I do understand the need for ensuring that we are not allowing people into the country who are terrorists or murderers,” Hanson said. “The reality is that immigrants comprise a much lower percentage of crimes than the overall population.”

Hanson said her perspective toward immigrants is shaped in part by her family history. Her grandfather was initially denied entry to the United States after fleeing Poland in the 1920s. But he entered anyway. Hanson believes that had he gone back, he would’ve perished in the Holocaust.

“I wouldn’t exist if he hadn’t been allowed into the U.S,” Hanson said. “I’m eternally grateful that he made it here, eventually became a citizen, and built a family and business and contributed to [the] community.”

Levi Sweeney, 30, Skyway, WA

“I keep saying, immigration is not my number one problem, but I've never met an immigrant I didn't like.”

Levi Sweeney refers to himself as a “dyed-in-the-wool Republican.” He voted for Trump in 2024, although not with much enthusiasm. He calls Trump “the best of a bunch of bad options.”

Sweeney currently works as a janitor in his family’s printing business. He is also a writer and self-publishes his novels.

He said he believes immigration policy under Trump is “going in the right direction, more or less.” He describes the Biden administration immigration policy as “lax.”

He believes “illegal immigrants who are career criminals should absolutely be deported.”

But he is more circumspect about people who are in the country without authorization but who “have a clean record, who are just regular guys and gals, who have held down jobs and contributed to their community.”

“[They] should of course be given leniency,” he said.

But that would mean changing immigration policies to allow for workers to come to the U.S. legally, Sweeney said.

“I would love it if they could live in this country legally, and could easily migrate here without breaking any laws,” he said.

Sweeney doesn’t believe that many people voted for President Trump because he promised to crack down on illegal immigration. He believes most were concerned about bread and butter issues, like the economy, jobs, and housing.

In terms of the people who are being arrested on the streets by ICE, he said it's unfortunate.

“I'd prefer it didn't have to happen at all, to be frank,” he said.

Leona Oliveros, 33, Federal Way, WA

“The movement of people is usually part of a bigger system, bigger injustice that we might not be able to see individually… but it’s there.”

As a history teacher, immigration is top of mind for Leona Oliveros. She teaches at Highline College where about a third of the students enrolled are not U.S.-born citizens.

Oliveros said she makes room for them to talk about their families’ immigration stories to help them see there’s no standard experience.

“Some of my students, there can be tension when talking about immigration, legal versus illegal, like, ‘Why would you do it this way, I had to do it the legal way?’” she said.

That sentiment resonates within her family, according to Oliveros. Like many of her older family members, her parents came to the U.S. from the Philippines by enlisting in the military; it was a pathway to citizenship.

“There’s this assumption that all other undocumented immigration is like jumping the border and the desert and not having the empathy to see that it’s not as simple as that,” she said.

Oliveros sees how current ICE enforcements are affecting students on campus. When word gets out about potential ICE sightings or activities around the area, students don’t come to school or they worry about how to get to work.

“I hate seeing that kind of anxiety among my student body,” Oliveros said. “What’s the American dream if we’re also making it harder to do?”

Actual Article Body:
Supporters of the White House barely showed up in replies to its latest post about election fraud, as critics claimed its “bots” vanished after drones hit a Russian data center.

“Under President Trump, criminals who disrupt the integrity of America’s elections will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” the White House wrote on X Monday.

The post shared a Justice Department announcement of charges against 16 people accused of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration and related election crimes.

A Raw Story review of the 176 most relevant replies Monday found that 138 opposed or mocked the White House. Only 19 backed it, and 19 more could not be classified.

“So Trump and Elon are going to jail?” one user asked.

“Hey! Where’d all the bots go?!?” another user wrote.

“Are you sad your RUSSIAN bot farms were destroyed?” a third user asked.

“Sixteen down, tens of thousands to go!” wrote one of the few users who backed the White House.

“Holy s— read the comments. The bots are completely gone,” Quadcarl, an X user with nearly 48,000 followers, wrote 22 minutes after the White House posted.

“Lmao usually these posts are filled with bootlicking bots….they’re all gone!” wrote the account Wu Tang is for the Children, which has more than 300,000 followers.

Their posts on X show the claim spread among popular accounts, but the posts are not evidence that it is true.

“Now that Russia data centers are getting pounded by Ukraine, your bots are going away,” another user replied to the White House.

Yandex, a Russian tech company sometimes called “Russia’s Google,” said Sunday that a drone attack completely shut down its data center in the Vladimir region, Reuters reported.

It was the third major Yandex data center knocked out in a few days, after strikes on sites in Sasovo and Kaluga, according to Reuters.

Yandex has blamed Ukraine for the Kaluga attack, but Ukraine has not officially claimed the strikes, The Deep Dive reported.

Automated traffic from Yandex’s network fell to near zero around the start of Oct. 11, according to Cloudflare Radar data cited by The Deep Dive. At one point that day, requests stood at 0.3% of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2% at the same hour a week earlier.

The Deep Dive writer JP Alegre cautioned that knocking out so much of Yandex’s infrastructure would likely cut automated requests even if no influence operation ran there.

“The chart can’t separate fewer bots from fewer working servers,” Alegre wrote.
